chapters.title: Chapter 5: Capstone - Building and Presenting Your Own Factor Strategy

lessons.title: Presenting Quant Research: What Interviewers and PMs Actually Want to See

body.text: A single, beautiful cumulative return chart proves you can make a chart look good. A structured writeup with a clear hypothesis, honest robustness checks, and a real limitations section proves you can think like a researcher, and that second thing is what an interviewer is actually screening for.

children.text: You have a well-scoped, falsifiable hypothesis and a plan for handling data limitations honestly. This lesson is about the last mile: packaging that research so a PM, interviewer, or prop desk reader can quickly see both what you found and how much they should trust it.
The Structure Every Quant Research Writeup Needs

body.caption: The six sections a quant research writeup should always include, in this order

cells: The specific, falsifiable question, stated in plain English before any data appears
Universe, data source, date range, exact metric definitions, breakpoints, and rebalancing frequency
The core finding, with risk-adjusted metrics, not just total return, and performance broken out by sub-period
How the result holds up under reasonable variations in the methodology's parameters
Data quality, survivorship bias, sample period, and cost assumption caveats, stated plainly
A direct answer to the original hypothesis, and what you would test next with more time or data

children.text: Lead With the Question, Not the Chart

A common, avoidable mistake is opening a presentation with a cumulative return chart before the reader even knows what question it is answering. A reader who has to guess the hypothesis from the chart is being asked to do your framing work for you, and most will simply disengage. State the hypothesis from Chapter 5's first lesson, in one or two plain sentences, before showing a single number.

body.text: Interviewers who evaluate research presentations regularly develop a fast heuristic: if the first slide or paragraph is a chart, the candidate is leading with a result they are excited about. If the first slide or paragraph is a question, the candidate is leading with a process they trust. The second impression is the one that gets you hired onto a research desk.

children.text: Show Robustness, Not Just the Best Result

Chapter 5's first lesson raised p-hacking directly: quietly trying several parameter variations and presenting only the best one. The direct antidote in a writeup is a robustness table, showing the same core finding tested across a small number of reasonable, pre-specified variations, rather than a single result presented as if it were the only version you ever tried.

body.caption: A hypothetical robustness check: does the conclusion survive different breakpoint choices?

children.text: Notice what this hypothetical table shows: the Sharpe ratio is not identical across breakpoints, and it should not be, but it stays positive and directionally consistent across all three reasonable choices, gradually declining as the selection broadens, exactly what you would expect if the effect is real rather than an artifact of one specific, cherry-picked cutoff. A robustness table that instead showed a strong result at the decile breakpoint and a near-zero or negative result at the tercile breakpoint would be a red flag for overfitting, not a footnote to skip past.

body.title: A Flattering Presentation vs an Honest One

columns.label: Flattering Presentation
points: One smooth cumulative return chart on a log scale, which visually compresses volatility and drawdowns
Only total or annualised return reported, no volatility or drawdown context
A single, full-period aggregate number, with no breakdown by market regime
No mention of transaction costs or capacity

columns.label: Honest Presentation
points: Cumulative return shown alongside a separate drawdown chart, so the pain, not just the payoff, is visible
Risk-adjusted metrics reported, Sharpe or Sortino ratio, alongside raw return
Performance broken out by sub-period or regime, echoing Chapter 2's lesson on factor cyclicality
Transaction cost assumptions and capacity limitations stated explicitly, alongside the headline result

children.text: A strong presenter addresses the obvious follow-up questions before being asked, rather than being visibly caught off guard by them.

body.caption: Common pushback questions and what a strong answer demonstrates

cells: You modelled costs from the start, per Chapter 3, rather than treating them as an afterthought
'How would this hold up out of sample, or in a different regime?'
You understand factor cyclicality (Chapter 2) and tested across sub-periods rather than relying on one lucky window
You pre-registered your methodology (Chapter 5) and can show the robustness checks that back that claim up

You understand liquidity and market impact (Chapter 2's size factor lesson, Chapter 4's implementation lesson) well enough to have an honest, reasoned estimate rather than an unexamined assumption of infinite scalability

body.title: Reviewing a Weak Writeup
body.scenario: A fellow learner shares their capstone writeup for feedback. It consists of a single slide: a smooth, upward-sloping cumulative return chart on a log scale, titled 'My Value Strategy Beats the Nifty 50', with a total return figure in large text and no other content.
body.prompt: Using the structure and honesty principles from this lesson, list at least four specific additions or changes you would recommend before they present this.
body.modelAnswer: At minimum: state the specific, falsifiable hypothesis being tested before showing any chart, rather than opening with the result. Add a separate drawdown chart alongside the cumulative return chart, since a log-scale cumulative return line can visually hide painful periods. Report a risk-adjusted metric like the Sharpe ratio, not just total return, since a higher return achieved with much higher volatility is not obviously a better outcome. Add a robustness section showing the result holds up, or does not, under at least one or two reasonable variations in methodology, and add an explicit limitations section covering data quality, survivorship bias if applicable, transaction costs, and the specific historical period tested. Without these additions, the writeup reads as a single flattering result rather than a piece of research an interviewer or PM could actually evaluate or trust.

body.title: Test Yourself: Reading a Robustness Table
body.question: In the hypothetical robustness table in this lesson, the Sharpe ratio declines gradually from 0.85 (top decile) to 0.79 (top quintile) to 0.71 (top tercile). What does this pattern suggest?
options: The result is likely an overfit artifact and should be discarded entirely
The effect appears directionally consistent and real, with the premium naturally moderating as the selection broadens to include less extreme stocks
The methodology is flawed because the Sharpe ratio is not identical across all three breakpoints
This pattern proves the strategy will definitely be profitable when traded live
body.explanation: A gradual, directionally consistent decline as the selection broadens from the most extreme decile to a wider tercile is exactly what you would expect from a genuine effect, since the most extreme names typically carry the strongest signal. A sharp reversal or a result that only appears at one specific, narrow breakpoint would be the actual red flag for overfitting, not this smooth pattern.

body.title: Vocabulary Check: Terms From This Lesson

cards.definition: Testing a core research finding across a small number of reasonable, pre-specified parameter variations to confirm it is not an artifact of one specific, cherry-picked choice.

A common charting choice that compresses the visual appearance of volatility and drawdowns, which can unintentionally (or intentionally) flatter a volatile strategy if shown without a separate risk or drawdown view.
Reporting a strategy's performance separately across distinct historical periods or macro regimes, rather than only a single full-period aggregate figure.

body.text: The robustness figures in this lesson are hypothetical, illustrating presentation principles only, not the actual results of any tested strategy. This lesson describes general research communication practices, not a guaranteed formula for interview success, which also depends on the specific role, firm, and interviewer.

points: A quant research writeup should follow a consistent structure: hypothesis, data and methodology, results, robustness checks, limitations, and conclusion, in that order
Lead with the specific hypothesis in plain English before showing any chart or number
A robustness table testing reasonable parameter variations is the direct, visible antidote to the p-hacking concern raised in this chapter's first lesson
Honest visualisation means showing drawdown alongside cumulative return, reporting risk-adjusted metrics, and breaking results out by sub-period or regime
Anticipating pushback on transaction costs, out-of-sample performance, data mining, and capacity demonstrates the same rigour this entire course has tried to model
The final lesson of this course turns this presentation skill into direct interview preparation, working through the specific questions this material is likely to generate
